title: Throughput harness calibration playbook for heterogeneous GPUs
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a tactical playbook for calibrating our throughput benchmarking harness when running across mixed GPU fleets (A100/RTX6000/H100/other partners). Goal: get repeatable, comparable throughput numbers while accounting for variable micro-thermal behavior, PCIe/NVLink differences, quantization code-path variance, and warmup sensitivity. This doc is intentionally pragmatic—checklists, salvage rules, and statistical gates rather than a long theory treatment.

High-level approach (summary):
- Treat the harness as a measurement instrument that must be calibrated per-machine-class and per-quantization-path.
- Separate stability verification into two stages: micro-prime (fast checks, O(minutes)) and macro-priming (long stabilization, O(hours)).
- Define "tolerances" for acceptable run noise and a tiebreaker arbitration for near-equal claims.
- Provide automated salvage steps to rescue runs contaminated by transient system noise.

Key concepts and vocabulary (team shorthand):
- micro-prime: quick, shallow warmup to validate kernel selection, batched kernel initialization, and shared memory ramps (10–90 sec).
- macro-prime: long warmup that exercises KV cache steady-state, I/O spikes, thermal drift (20–90 minutes depending on model length).
- calibration anchor: canonical input set + RNG seed set used as the canonical workload fingerprint for a machine class.
- salvage: a deterministic sequence of steps to either recover or abort a corrupted experiment run.
- tiebreaker: deterministic policy to prefer one run/system over another in near-equal throughput claims.

Procedure: pre-run checks (automated)
1) node health: verify driver, CUDA, NCCL versions match expected image. Fail fast if any mismatch.
   - command hints: nvidia-smi -q, nvprof --query, dpkg -l | grep nvidia
2) thermal baseline: snapshot GPU temp and power caps; if any device > 60C static before run -> reschedule.
3) neighbor-noise check: verify no high-priority processes are present (watch for checkpointing, backups, Kubectl log storms).
4) kernel inventory: record selected kernels and quantization paths from profiler output (store as JSON artifact).
5) filesystem: ensure model shard read-ahead and tmpfs mounting for KV cache as required.

Micro-prime (2-6 minutes):
- Purpose: verify deterministic kernel paths, check for immediate OOM/alloc hiccups, and ensure per-request p95 latency is within 5x of expected baseline.
- Steps:
  1) Run 50 short single-token requests using canonical anchor inputs at low concurrency (C=1).. record time-to-first-byte and token emission latency.
  2) Run 200 requests at target batch-size but at low arrival rate (to validate batching logic).
  3) Validate profiler traces: ensure no fallback to slow kernels and no repeated tiny memcpy patterns indicating PCIe thrash.
- Failure conditions and salvage:
  - If >10% allocations fail or if any request returns 500-level error -> abort and notify SRE.
  - If kernel fallback observed -> tag run as non-comparable, schedule targeted kernel-fix job.

Macro-prime (stabilization, 20–90 minutes):
- Purpose: let KV cache, batched executors, and thermal characteristics reach steady state so throughput can be measured reliably.
- Strategy: progressive concurrency ramp with anchored checkpoints:
  - Phase A (10 minutes): constant low concurrency ramp to warm KV and caches (C=1 -> C=4) with bursts every 2 minutes to engage batching.
  - Phase B (10–30 minutes): hold near-target concurrency but periodically inject micro-bursts (10–30% above target for 30s) to exercise backpressure and preemption paths.
  - Phase C (rest): sustained target concurrency for remainder of macro-prime.
- Observability to capture during macro-prime:
  - per-GPU utilization, temp, power draw
  - kernel selection timeline (per-minute snapshot)
  - request-level latencies (p50/p95/p99), queue lengths, batch sizes observed
  - system-level metrics (CPU steal, IRQ rates)

Load generator configs (suggested templates):
- anchor-small.json (for short-token models):
  - concurrency_target: 32
  - batch_target: 8
  - arrival_pattern: poisson
  - seed: 23917
  - steady_duration: 1800
  - microburst_schedule: every 5m, +20% for 45s

- anchor-long.json (for long-seq models):
  - concurrency_target: 12
  - batch_target: 4
  - arrival_pattern: steady-windowed
  - seed: 98213
  - steady_duration: 3600
  - microburst_schedule: every 10m, +25% for 60s

Repeatability and RNG hygiene:
- Always stamp the run with the seed and the anchor set name. Store the seed in the artifact bundle.
- Use deterministic text anchors (no sampling) for the primary claim run; sampling runs for stress tests are fine but must be tagged non-comparable.
- If stochastic components exist (e.g., temperature-dependent clock boosts), capture them and include them in the final report.

Noise detection and automatic gating rules (automated):
- Gate A: thermal drift detection. If median GPU temp increases >8C during macro-prime -> mark run noisy and trigger salvage.
- Gate B: p95 latency ramp. If p95 increases >2x relative to micro-prime baseline -> inspect for kernel fallback and I/O stalls.
- Gate C: batch size entropy. If observed batch size distribution deviates from target distribution by >15% for >3 consecutive windows -> tag run and either salvage or resample.

Salvage procedure (deterministic):
1) dump artifacts (profiler traces, nvidia-smi logs, dmesg).
2) attempt soft-recover: pause for 5m, cool-down fans allowed to run, clear OS caches, remount tmpfs for KV cache, restart loadgen clients with same seed and resume macro-prime for additional 30 minutes.
   - If soft-recover returns metrics within tolerances -> label run as "rescued" and include rescue log in artifacts.
3) if soft-recover fails, hard-recover: reboot node (or reschedule container), rerun micro-prime, then macro-prime. Tag run as "after-reboot".
4) if repeated hard-recover fails >2 times across the same machine class -> quarantine machine and open SRV-1428 (example) for infra investigation.

Tiebreaker policy for close throughput claims (deterministic ranking):
- Primary: mean throughput across last 10 minutes of steady window (higher wins).
- Secondary: p95 latency (lower wins).
- Tertiary: kernel fidelity score (count of non-fallback kernel invocations; higher wins).
- Quaternary: energy efficiency (tokens / watt-minute).
- If still tied, deterministic fallback to lexicographic order of machine serials to avoid flapping claims.

Statistical tests and sample sizing notes:
- Use bootstrapped confidence intervals on median throughput. For most models, 30 minutes of steady-state sampling gives useful CI widths. For heavy tails or microburst-sensitive workloads, use 60–90 minutes.
- When comparing two machine classes, run at least n=5 independent steady-state samples (different seeds and anchor subsets) to get robust p-values. Use non-parametric Mann-Whitney U for throughput comparisons.

Artifacts to store with every run (mandatory):
- loadgen config JSON (with seed)
- profiler timeline (per-GPU kernel list)
- nvidia-smi CSV (1s resolution)
- batch size histogram (minute windows)
- raw request logs (anonymized ids)
- environment snapshot (driver/cuda/nccl/docker image)
- short human-readable run_summary.md with gate results and any salvage actions applied

Reporting template (sparse):
- run_id: <uuid>
- anchor_name: <canonical set>
- machine_class: <A100-80GB-x2>
- claim_throughput: <tokens/sec> +/- <CI>
- p50/p95/p99: <ms>
- gates: PASS|NOISY|FAILED (list gates triggered)
- salvage: none|soft-recover|after-reboot (include notes)
- linked_artifacts: artifact bundle path

Operational notes and pitfalls we've hit (lessons):
- NVLink topology differences cause silent variance in kernel selection for fused attention kernels; always tag runs with topology.
- Preemptible neighbor workloads (k8s best-effort pods) can pollute runs even when not obviously busy; the neighbor-noise check should include kernel-level contention signals.
- Quantized int8 paths can show non-linear thermal sensitivity because of different memory access patterns; treat quantized vs fp16 as separate machine-class runs unless proven identical.
- Small models (short seq) are dominated by scheduler latency; batching heuristics matter more than raw kernel throughput.

TODOs and open questions:
- Add automated energy-capture hook for cloud provider billing APIs (tracked in JIRA: SRV-1763).
- Formalize batch-size entropy metric and add a Grafana panel for it.
- Investigate whether we can use hardware power caps as a stability knob during long runs (pro/con: hides real behavior).

Quick checklist for running a claim (copy/paste):
- [ ] ensure image + drivers match benchmark image tag
- [ ] pick canonical anchor and seed
- [ ] push micro-prime; wait for micro-probe gates
- [ ] if micro-prime OK -> start macro-prime
- [ ] monitor gates; if gate trips apply salvage
- [ ] if run completes, upload artifacts and fill run_summary.md

Notes-to-self: keep the salvage steps deterministic and fully logged. If a run is rescued, don't silently upgrade it to a clean claim — it must be flagged in the registry and downstream dashboards need to be able to filter rescued runs out of leaderboard views.

References and links:
- See Confluence: SERVE-Perf-Playbook-2025 (link above) for background and other tuning knobs.
- Related Jira: SRV-1428 (noisy-A100-thermal) and SRV-1763 (energy-capture).
- PR: github.com/redwood-inference/bench-harness/pull/384 contains the micro-prime orchestrator patch.

If you're running this for a first-of-class machine, ping @Maya for topology checklist and @Diego for NVLink tracing tips.

-- Priya (benchmarking lead, eng-serving-runtime)
